\section{The forecast and its presentation to Parliament}
\label{sec:lttv-forecast}

In March 2015 the CRTC told television distributors to offer, by March 2016, an entry-level service \enquote{priced at no more than \$25 (not including equipment) per month} \citep[para.~26]{crtc2015worldofchoice}. Every discretionary channel was to be available on its own or in small packages by March 2016, and in both forms by December 2016 \citep[para.~47]{crtc2015worldofchoice}. The policy came out of the \textit{Let's Talk TV} proceeding, at which, by one later account, \enquote{virtually all parties expressed concerns about potential impacts of unbundling} \citep[para.~xxii, p.~5]{nordicity2015television}.

Nordicity and Peter Miller's \textit{Canadian Television 2020}, dated December 2015, was prepared for ACTRA, the Canadian Media Guild, the Directors Guild of Canada, Friends of Canadian Broadcasting and Unifor \citep{nordicity2015television}. It modelled two worlds from 2015 to 2020: a baseline with \enquote{technological and consumer behaviour changes, assuming that the pre-existing broadcasting regulatory regime remains}, and the same world with the CRTC's decisions overlaid \citep[para.~ii, p.~1]{nordicity2015television}. I call these the report's baseline and its reform scenario; the forecast is the gap between them, and a quantity's path under the reform scenario is its reform path. A third scenario, with the decisions modified, isn't checked here.

By 2020, the report concluded, the decisions were \enquote{likely to result in a loss of 15,130 FTEs of employment in the Canadian economy}, counted in full-time equivalents (FTEs), along with \$\lttvGDPTotal{} million of GDP. Of those jobs, \lttvJobsDirect{} were directly in broadcasting and production and \lttvJobsSpinoff{} were spin-off employment, the indirect and induced employment in other sectors \citep[para.~xliv and Table~1 with its note, p.~12]{nordicity2015television}. The report also divides the total by the sector whose losses give rise to it: \lttvFTEProd{} to independent production (\lttvFTEProdDirect{} direct, \lttvFTEProdSpin{} spin-off) and \lttvFTEBroadcast{} to broadcasting (\lttvFTEBroadcastDirect{} direct, \lttvFTEBroadcastSpin{} spin-off) (table~\ref{tab:jobs-reconciliation}; \citealp[paras.~246, 248, 250; Tables~22--23, pp.~90--92]{nordicity2015television}). The \lttvFTESpecProd{} (\lttvFTESpecProdShare{}) attributed to specialty and pay services and to production depend in the model on those services' revenue and on spending on Canadian programming, which is why specialty and pay revenue is the main test below.

Those figures sit at the end of a chain. Subscribers move to cheaper unbundled packages; distributors lose retail revenue and pass most of the loss to Canadian channels as lower wholesale fees; weaker channels close; spending on Canadian programming falls; and input-output multipliers turn the spending into jobs and GDP. The report states the assumptions that drive each link. Subscribers taking the entry-level package with chosen channels, which the report calls Build Your Own Package (BYOP), make up \lttvByopSixteen{} of all subscribers in 2016, \lttvByopSeventeen{} in 2017 and \lttvByopEighteen{} from 2018 \citep[para.~202, Table~18, p.~76]{nordicity2015television}; I call this the report's BYOP uptake. Distributors pass \enquote{75\% of their retail revenue loss to Canadian programming services}, having attributed \lttvReportCanShare{} of that loss to Canadian services \citep[paras.~206--207, p.~77]{nordicity2015television}. By 2020, \lttvReportClosuresVI{} of the large integrated companies' Category A and B channels close, and \lttvReportClosuresIndep{} of the independents' \citep[paras.~232--233, p.~85]{nordicity2015television}.

By 2020 the reform path runs \$\lttvSpecImpactTwenty{} million (\lttvSpecShareTwenty{}) a year below the baseline for the revenue of specialty and pay services (\enquote{channels}, for short, below) and \$\lttvBDUImpactTwenty{} million (\lttvBDUShareTwenty{}) below it for distributors' revenue \citep[paras.~xxvi--xxvii]{nordicity2015television}. Canadian programming expenditure (CPE), which in the report includes distributors' contributions as well as programming services' spending, runs \$\lttvCPEImpactTwenty{} million below.

\subsection{What the committee heard}

On 12 April 2016 Ian Morrison of Friends of Canadian Broadcasting, accompanied by Miller, put the report to the Commons Standing Committee on Canadian Heritage. Its key findings, he said, were that \enquote{by 2020, some 15,130 media jobs will be lost}, along with \enquote{a \$400-million drop in Canadian program expenditures} that was \enquote{18\% of what now exists}, \enquote{all of this as the direct result of Let's Talk TV regulatory changes}. He added that the authors had \enquote{advanced proposals to reduce the negative impact of the CRTC's decisions by as much as 75\%} \citep[time marks 0900--0905]{commons2016chpc8}.

Two of these phrases depart from the report. The \lttvJobsTotal{} FTEs are economy-wide, and \lttvJobsSpinoff{} of them are spin-off employment in other sectors, so \enquote{media jobs} misdescribes them; and the report describes its \lttvCPEShareStated{} as a share of projected 2020 baseline spending, not of current spending. The \$400 million rounds the report's \$399 million, and \enquote{direct result} attributes the losses to the decisions, as the report does, though \enquote{will be lost} is firmer than the report's \enquote{likely}. The 18\% itself is the report's, and its own figures don't reproduce it. The report's own baseline figures put 2020 CPE at \$\lttvCPEBaselineTwenty{} million, so its \$\lttvCPEImpactTwenty{} million reduction is \lttvCPEShareTwenty{} of baseline, not the \lttvCPEShareStated{} its text states \citep[para.~239; Figs.~8, 9, 43]{nordicity2015television}. Against the report's own forecast for 2015, the reduction is \lttvCPEShareFifteen{}, and against what existed when Morrison spoke, the CRTC's count of 2015 spending (\$\lttvCPECRTCFifteen{} million), it's \lttvCPEShareCRTCFifteen{} \citep{crtc2017sfs2016}. None of the \lttvCPENCandidates{} shares tested, built from the report's figures over \lttvCPENDenominators{} denominators and its two impact figures, gives \lttvCPEShareStated{} (table~\ref{tab:cpe-denominators}).

Responding to a question about the \$25 bundle, one month after the entry-level service launched, Morrison cited a much lower uptake figure than the report's: \enquote{the best estimates I've seen, Mr.~Waugh, are that about 4\% of Canadians will go for it} \citep[time marks 0920--0925]{commons2016chpc8}. He didn't say how it bore on the job estimate, and \enquote{4\% of Canadians} doesn't specify a denominator.

\section{Comparing outcomes with the report's reform paths}
\label{sec:lttv-method}

The prediction record (forecasters, quantities, paths by year, stated assumptions) was committed before any CRTC outcome series was downloaded. I then re-read the report's two paths from the data labels on its charts, checking every value against the totals in its text, and ran a design analysis by fake-data simulation before opening any CRTC outcome file \citep{gelman2014types, gelman2020workflow}. It asked, for each forecast quantity, whether the outcome could separate a world in which the report's impact occurred from one in which it didn't, given that the baseline itself could be wrong.

That last clause is the hard part. In retrospective analysis of regulation, \enquote{developing a credible counterfactual is the most demanding aspect}, and the baselines assumed beforehand \enquote{must be revisited} to see whether outside factors changed the result \citep[286]{morgenstern2018retrospective}. Here the counterfactual is the report's own baseline, itself a forecast of how television would have fared under streaming without the reforms. So the check treats the baseline's error as unknown and reports results across a range of assumed scales for it. \textcite{kane2026sffa} varies the baseline period against which forecasts are judged; here the baseline is the report's own, and what varies is how wrong it's assumed to be.

With the annual error scale set to the historical volatility of the report's own 2010--2014 data, the design analysis classified specialty and pay revenue correctly in about \lttvDesignCorrectSpec{} of simulated worlds and distributors' revenue in about \lttvDesignCorrectBDU{}. CPE, whose historical volatility was \lttvHistSDCPE{} a year, came out at \lttvDesignCorrectCPE{}, so it was set aside in advance as descriptive.

For each revenue series I estimate a forecast scale \(k\). In logs, \(\log B_t-\log Y_t=k\,\delta_t+e_t\), where \(B_t\) is the report's baseline, \(Y_t\) the outcome, \(\delta_t\) the report's forecast shortfall (how far the reform path lies below the baseline) and \(e_t\) the baseline's error (positive when the baseline overstates what would have happened without the decisions), modelled as a random walk from 2014. So \(k=0\) corresponds to the baseline and \(k=1\) to the reform path, with baseline error in either case. I write \(\hat k\) for the estimate over 2016--2019, the four years before the pandemic, and \(k^{u}\) for the value a recalculated scenario implies. Because the baseline's error accumulates from year to year, \(\hat k\) rests on changes in the gap between outcome and baseline rather than on its level: for specialty and pay revenue it's positive although that revenue stayed above the baseline in every year, because its excess over the baseline shrank, the direction the reform path predicted. The report's paths and the CRTC series are both in nominal dollars, and since \(k\) compares them year by year, deflating both by the same price index leaves it unchanged.

The 95\% interval for \(k\) comes from generalized least squares under that model, and it reflects only the assumed error in the baseline, so its width depends on the annual error scale \(\sigma\). That scale is calibrated from an outside comparison, described below, rather than estimated from four years of outcomes, and the CRTC's administrative totals are treated as measured without error (appendix~\ref{app:methods}; inputs in table~\ref{tab:inputs}). The interval treats \(\sigma\) as known. Treating it as uncertain would widen the intervals; in the illustration in appendix~\ref{app:methods}, the distributors' interval then includes zero.

\(k\) compares the outcome with the report's two paths; it isn't an estimate of the decisions' causal effect, which would need a better counterfactual than the report's own baseline. I also construct a cited-input band for \(k\) by scaling the report's uptake-related components, in every year, by the ratio of each cited estimate (\lttvCitedUptakeLow{} and \lttvCitedUptakeHigh{}) to the report's \lttvByopEighteen{}, which keeps the report's ramp, and by multiplying closures by \lttvCitedClosuresMult{} in the high case. The band spans the values of \(k\) the report's cited estimates imply; it isn't a probability interval. The plan's verdicts compare the interval with that band; the verdict \enquote{forecast exceeded}, for example, applies only if the interval lies wholly above it.

The outcome series alone can't identify how wrong the baseline was, so the plan fixed an external check: the forecast of US Netflix subscribers that the report used for its US comparison (from Trefis), assumed unaffected by Canadian regulation, against Netflix's reported US paid memberships \citep{netflix2019form10k}. The report forecast \lttvNetflixFcEighteen{} million for 2018 and Netflix reported \lttvNetflixObsEighteen{} million, which gives a Netflix-derived annual scale of \lttvSigmaTech{}, below the historical volatility of both revenue series. Under the pre-stated rule the larger of the two sets \(\sigma\), so the designated error scale is the historical volatility, \lttvSigmaReadSpec{} for specialty and pay revenue and \lttvSigmaReadBDU{} for distributors' revenue. The CRTC series reproduce the report's 2012--2014 values within \lttvSpliceTol{} \citep{crtc2017sfs2016, crtc2021sfs2020}.

\section{Revenue outcomes and their sensitivity to baseline error}
\label{sec:lttv-results}

\subsection{Against the report's paths}

Figure~\ref{fig:paths} shows each revenue series against the report's two paths. Specialty and pay revenue stayed above the report's baseline, by between \lttvSpecVsBaselineMin{} and \lttvSpecVsBaselineMax{} from 2016 to 2019, and ran between \lttvSpecVsLTTVMin{} and \lttvSpecVsLTTVMax{} \lttvSpecAboveLTTV{} the reform path. Taken alone, the revenue \lttvSpecRevNomDir{} \lttvSpecRevNomChange{} in nominal dollars from 2015 to 2019 and \lttvSpecRevRealChange{} after inflation, while the report's baseline was flat in nominal dollars over 2016--2019 (table~\ref{tab:inputs}).

\begin{figure}[tbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/lttv_paths.pdf}
\caption{Revenue relative to the report's baseline, 2012--2019, in per cent of the baseline. The reform path and the baseline are the report's (Figs.~41, 42); the partial recalculation holds BYOP uptake at the CRTC's June 2016 entry-level share and the exemption-order and closure dollar components fixed (post hoc); the outcome is the CRTC series (2016 edition to 2015, 2020 edition after; specialty and pay services exclude exempt services). The shaded range is the pointwise 95\% range around the baseline under the error model at the designated error scale (\lttvSigmaReadSpec{} and \lttvSigmaReadBDU{} a year). Before 2015 the baseline is the report's own actual values. Both panels share one scale.}
\label{fig:paths}
\end{figure}

At the designated error scale \(\hat k=\lttvKSpec\), with a standard error of \lttvKSpecSE{}. That's \lttvKSpecSEsFromZero{} standard errors from \(k=0\) and \lttvKSpecSEsFromOne{} from \(k=1\), and the cited-input band's lower end, \lttvBandSpecLo{}, is \lttvKSpecSEsFromBandLo{} standard errors away. Under the pre-stated rule the verdict is \emph{smaller}: the 95\% interval, \lttvKSpecLoTwo{} to \lttvKSpecHiTwo{}, lies wholly below the band of \lttvBandSpecLo{} to \lttvBandSpecHi{}, so the outcome is incompatible with the reform path at the report's assumed uptake.

Distributors' revenue ran between \lttvBDUVsLTTVMin{} and \lttvBDUVsLTTVMax{} \lttvBDUAboveLTTV{} the report's reform path, falling from \$\lttvBDURevFifteen{} million in 2015 to \$\lttvBDURevNineteen{} million in 2019, a nominal decline of \lttvBDURevNomChange{}, or \lttvBDURevRealChange{} after inflation. Here \(\hat k=\lttvKBDU\) (standard error \lttvKBDUSE{}), \lttvKBDUSEsFromZero{} standard errors from \(k=0\) and \lttvKBDUSEsFromOne{} from \(k=1\). Its interval, \lttvKBDULoTwo{} to \lttvKBDUHiTwo{}, includes \(k=1\) and overlaps the band of \lttvBandBDULo{} to \lttvBandBDUHi{}, so under the pre-stated rule the verdict is \emph{consistent}.

\subsection{Uptake: the report's assumption and the evidence}

The report took its \lttvByopEighteen{} from outside estimates, the highest being Oliver Wyman's finding that \enquote{as many as 35\% of subscribers would be willing to switch to a skinny-basic/BYOP option} \citep[para.~201, p.~75]{nordicity2015television}. The CRTC counted more than \lttvUptakeAprilN{} subscribers to the entry-level package five weeks after launch \citep{crtc2016basicpackage} and \lttvUptakeJuneN{} by 30 June 2016 \citep[para.~12]{crtc2016hearing0907}, about \lttvUptakeAprilShare{} and \lttvUptakeJuneShare{} of the 2016 subscriber total. These count subscribers to the entry-level package with or without added channels, a different measure from the report's BYOP uptake, taken before every channel had to be offered singly as well as in small packages; I found no later CRTC count. A survey by the Media Technology Monitor, released in August 2017, put adoption of starter packages at \enquote{just over 1 in 10 TV subscribers} and, separately, reported that 29\% of subscribers were adding individual channels or bundles to their packages \citep{mtm2017starter}. Surveys aren't among the sources the analysis plan accepted for uptake. This one is self-reported, gives no fieldwork dates, sample size or margin of error, and may not measure the report's BYOP share, so it's reported beside the planned reading. The survey path below reads its \enquote{just over 1 in 10} as 10\%, a floor, and assumes that level held from 2017 through 2019.

Low uptake in 2016 may partly reflect how the package was sold, a possibility the report itself raised, that distributors might offer unbundling in a way \enquote{relatively unattractive from a price-value equation, so that very few Canadians opt for it} \citep[para.~78, n.~40, p.~34]{nordicity2015television}. The CRTC's hearing of September 2016 examined \enquote{the practices certain providers have adopted in offering} it \citep[para.~5]{crtc2016hearing0907}. Uptake in mid-2016 was far below the report's 2016 assumption; whether it stayed low is what the survey puts in doubt.

\subsection{Partial recalculations under assumed uptake paths}

To ask what the report's chain implies at other uptake levels, I rescale each year's unbundling and preponderance components by the assumed BYOP share over the report's (Table~18) and hold the exemption-order and closure dollar components fixed. The report values those two components partly from the others \citep[paras.~220, 234]{nordicity2015television}, so the recalculation is partial; its scenario coefficient \(k^{u}\) is the recalculated shortfall path projected in the same way as the band. Table~\ref{tab:scenarios-main} shows four uptake paths, and table~\ref{tab:scenarios} all seven. The paths were added after the outcome data was opened, and the survey path uses a source outside the plan's (table~\ref{tab:chronology}).

\input{sections/table-scenarios-main}

With uptake held at the CRTC's June 2016 share, \(k^{u}=\lttvKPredSpecObsUptake\) for specialty and pay revenue, compatible with \(\hat k\) at the designated error scale (\lttvKPredSpecObsUptakeSEs{} standard errors away), and \lttvKPredBDUObsUptake{} for distributors, \lttvKPredBDUObsUptakeSEs{} standard errors below \(\hat k\), a gap that falls below two with the 2017 or pooled calibration, the rescaled series or the offset model (\lttvBDUGapSEsSeventeen{}, \lttvBDUGapSEsPooled{}, \lttvBDUGapSEsRescaled{} and \lttvBDUGapSEsOffset{}). On the survey path, 1.6\% in 2016 and 10\% from 2017, \(k^{u}=\lttvKPredSpecSurvey\) for specialty and pay revenue, \lttvKPredSpecSurveySEs{} standard errors above \(\hat k\), though below the interval's upper end at the largest calibrated error scale (\lttvKSpecHiWidest{}), and \lttvKPredBDUSurvey{} for distributors, \lttvKPredBDUSurveySEs{} standard errors below. A linear rise from 1.6\% to \lttvMorrisonUptake{} by 2019 gives \lttvKPredSpecRiseMorrison{} and \lttvKPredBDURiseMorrison{}, both inside their intervals. Among the paths tested, at the designated error scale, that rise is the only one that keeps both series compatible with the partial recalculation; larger error scales widen the set.

The recalculations don't fall to zero because the two fixed components don't scale with uptake: closures, and the exemption order for broadcasters' streaming services, which the report expected to \enquote{materially increase cord cutting and cord shaving} \citep[para.~xxiii]{nordicity2015television}.

\subsection{Distributors' revenue by subscribers and revenue per subscriber}

Splitting distributors' revenue into subscribers and revenue per subscriber locates their shortfall. The report's components act on different factors: unbundling lowers revenue per subscriber and leaves subscriber numbers alone, while the exemption order adds cord cutting, 1.9\% of subscribers a year against 1.5\% in the baseline \citep[paras.~204--205, 216, 220; Tables~5, 21]{nordicity2015television}. Rebuilding the report's exemption-order component from its stated cord cutting and cord shaving reproduces it to within about \lttvDecCheckMaxDev{} in every year, so the reform scenario's split can be recovered (table~\ref{tab:decomposition}).

The comparison is of changes from 2014, since in the report's actual years the CRTC's subscriber counts sit \lttvDecSubAlignLo{} to \lttvDecSubAlignHi{} below the report's and its revenue per subscriber \lttvDecPerAlignLo{} to \lttvDecPerAlignHi{} above. It assumes the two series stay comparable after 2014: the report's subscriber series includes \enquote{non-reporting BDUs} (Fig.~17; BDUs, broadcasting distribution undertakings, is the CRTC's term for distributors), the CRTC's cover broadcast years ending 31 August, and revenue per subscriber here is total distributor revenue, which is broader than a package price.

By 2019, measured this way, subscribers had fallen a further \lttvDecSubObs{} below the report's baseline path, against \lttvDecSubFc{} in its reform scenario. Revenue per subscriber was \lttvDecPerObs{} below the baseline path, against \lttvDecPerFc{} in the reform scenario: it rose only \lttvRevPerSubObsGrowth{} in nominal dollars, from \$\lttvRevPerSubFourteen{} a month in 2014 to \$\lttvRevPerSubNineteen{} in 2019 (\lttvRevPerSubRealFall{} lower after inflation), while the baseline path rose \lttvRevPerSubBaseGrowth{}; its underlying price assumption was inflation plus one point, before an allowance for cord shaving \citep[Table~11, paras.~151--152]{nordicity2015television}. With uptake held at the June 2016 share, the partial recalculation gives a per-subscriber shortfall of \lttvDecPerCounted{}, and on the survey path \lttvDecPerSurvey{}. Of the total revenue shortfall, in logs and measured from 2014, \lttvDecBeyondCounted{} exceeds the partial recalculation with uptake held at 1.6\% and \lttvDecBeyondSurvey{} on the survey path. In nominal terms distributors' revenue fell \lttvBDURevFallFourteenNineteen{} from 2014 to 2019, as subscribers fell \lttvSubsFallFourteenNineteen{} and revenue per subscriber rose \lttvRevPerSubObsGrowth{}; against the report's rising baseline, about \lttvDecPerShare{} of the shortfall, in logs, is missing growth in revenue per subscriber.

The split was added after the outcome data was opened, under a rule fixed before it was computed (table~\ref{tab:chronology}); the comparisons with uptake held at 1.6\% and on the survey path go beyond that rule. It's an accounting identity, and revenue per subscriber is computed from the same totals, so the split locates the shortfall without observing prices or identifying causes. Subscriber losses exceed those in both of the report's paths compared here, and stagnant revenue per subscriber could reflect pricing, cord shaving to smaller packages, or the reforms themselves.

\subsection{Sensitivity to the error scale}

\begin{figure}[tbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/lttv_k_sigma.pdf}
\caption{The estimate \(\hat k\) and its 95\% interval as a function of the annual error scale of the report's baseline, \(\sigma\), the standard deviation of the yearly changes in its error. The solid vertical line marks the designated error scale; dotted lines mark the values of \(\sigma\) used by the other calibrations (table~\ref{tab:calibrations}). The grey band is the cited-input band. The horizontal axis spans the plan's sensitivity range, 1\% to 8\% a year; intervals are conditional on \(\sigma\). The standard error is proportional to \(\sigma\), so the interval widens linearly while the estimate stays put.}
\label{fig:k-sigma}
\end{figure}

Both intervals depend on the error scale (figure~\ref{fig:k-sigma}). The estimates don't move as the assumed scale increases; the intervals widen in proportion. The specialty and pay interval reaches the cited-input band when the scale reaches about \lttvCutoffSpec{} a year, and at the largest calibrated scale, \lttvSigmaWidest{}, its upper end is \lttvKSpecHiWidest{}. The distributors' interval includes zero from about \lttvCutoffBDU{}. At the plan's upper value of 8\% a year, the specialty and pay interval, \lttvKSpecLoEight{} to \lttvKSpecHiEight{}, includes \(k=1\). None of the reported specialty and pay intervals excludes zero. The verdict labels in table~\ref{tab:calibrations} change as the assumed scale crosses these values while the estimate stays the same \citep{gelmanStern2006difference}. Several calibrations were added after the outcome data was opened, so all of them are shown \citep{gelman2014statcrisis}.

The pre-stated Netflix comparison gives a scale of \lttvSigmaTech{} a year, below both series' historical volatility, so the historical volatility sets the designated scale. Other defensible readings of the comparison give more: the 2016 miss gives a Netflix-derived scale of \lttvSigmaTechSixteen{} a year and a pooled estimate \lttvSigmaTechPooled{}. Part of the 2016 miss is an inherited offset, since the report's 2015 starting figure (\lttvNetflixFcFifteen{} million) was already above Netflix's count (\lttvNetflixObsFifteen{} million) \citep{netflix2018form10k}. Measured as growth, Netflix's memberships outran the Trefis forecast the report used, by \lttvNetflixObsGrowth{} against \lttvNetflixFcGrowth{} from 2015 to 2018, which gives a scale of \lttvSigmaGrowthEighteen{} a year.

\subsection{Checking the error model}

A check of the statistical error model, added after the outcome data was opened, finds the specialty and pay residual concentrated in its first step. After fitting \(k\), the standardized changes in the baseline's error between observations are correlated and have variances below one. Divided by their standard deviations under the fit, the specialty and pay step from 2014 to 2016 is \lttvInnovSpecFirst{}, and the largest of the three later steps is \lttvInnovSpecLaterMax{} in absolute value; the distributors' steps show no such pattern. A one-time gap between the report's baseline and the CRTC series would produce this, though with four points so would a random walk whose later steps happened to be small.

Part of the specialty and pay gap is already visible in 2015, a year with no forecast impact, in the report's own figure for that year (itself a forecast). The CRTC later counted \$\lttvCRTCFifteenSpec{} million, \lttvGapFifteenSpec{} \lttvGapFifteenSpecDir{} the report's \$\lttvReportFifteenSpec{} million, against \lttvGapFourteenSpec{} in 2014 and negligible differences in 2012 and 2013, when the report's figures were actuals. Distributors' revenue shows no such change: the CRTC's counts run between \lttvGapRangeLoBDU{} and \lttvGapRangeHiBDU{} \lttvGapFifteenBDUDir{} the report's figures in every year from 2012 to 2015, a standing difference between the two series, with no new divergence in 2015. The 2016 and 2020 editions of the CRTC's summaries differ on 2016 by \lttvReleaseGapSpec{} for specialty and pay services and \lttvReleaseGapBDU{} for distributors, so revisions between editions can't account for the gap. Allowing a level offset in the error model, which absorbs both, gives \(\hat k=\lttvKSpecOffset\) (standard error \lttvKSpecOffsetSE{}) for specialty and pay revenue and \lttvKBDUOffset{} (\lttvKBDUOffsetSE{}) for distributors' revenue, leaving both pre-stated verdicts as they were; the distributors' comparison with uptake held at 1.6\% falls to \lttvBDUGapSEsOffset{} standard errors.

\section{Payments, closures and staff counts}
\label{sec:lttv-links}

\subsection{Payments to Canadian channels}

The report also assumed a path for what distributors pay Canadian channels. In its baseline the monthly carriage fee per subscriber for Canadian specialty and pay services rises \lttvBaseFeeGrowth{} from 2015 to 2019 \citep[Table~14, p.~67]{nordicity2015television}, and under the decisions it falls below that path as distributors pass on \lttvReportPassThrough{} of the retail loss attributed to Canadian services. What distributors paid Canadian channels in affiliation payments rose from \$\lttvPayCanFifteen{} million in 2015 to \$\lttvPayCanNineteen{} million in 2019 while subscribers fell, so per subscriber it rose \lttvPerSubGrowth{}, and the Canadian share of all affiliation payments stayed near \lttvPayShareFifteen{} \citep[Table~U-T11]{crtc2019cmrbdu}. After inflation the total \lttvPayCanRealDir{} \lttvPayCanRealChange{} and the payment per subscriber \lttvPerSubRealDir{} \lttvPerSubRealChange{}; the comparison with the report's fee path needs no such adjustment, since that path is nominal too.

The report's carriage fee per subscriber and the CRTC's affiliation payments divided by subscribers differ by definition, so their growth is compared, not their levels. With uptake near the CRTC's 2016 share there would have been little loss to pass on, and the comparison would mainly show that payments grew faster than the report's baseline assumed; on the survey path, the partial recalculation has fees falling relative to the baseline path, and observed payments instead grew faster than it. The aggregates can't say what fees would have been without the decisions, or why affiliation payments per subscriber rose. Some of the payments stay inside the integrated groups, and the report itself expected the exemption order's impact on those groups to be partly offset by their streaming and broadband revenue \citep[para.~227, p.~83]{nordicity2015television}. The CRTC's wholesale code, scheduled to take effect in January 2016 \citep[p.~73, n.~82]{nordicity2015television}, is in both of the report's scenarios \citep[p.~72, n.~80]{nordicity2015television}, so its fee path already allows for it.

\subsection{Closures}

For the integrated companies, closures came out close to the report: between \lttvClosVILo{} and \lttvClosVIHi{} of their Category A and B channels stopped operating by 2019--2020, against the report's \lttvReportClosuresVI. For the independents the bounds, \lttvClosIndLo{} to \lttvClosIndHi{}, contain the report's \lttvReportClosuresIndep{} but are too wide to test it, because in the summaries used here channels that continued under an exemption from individual licensing can't be told apart from channels that closed. Both ranges classify Corus, which owns the former Shaw Media channels in the 2016 data, as independent; counted as integrated, as the analysis plan also required, it gives \lttvClosVICorusLo{} to \lttvClosVICorusHi{} for the integrated companies and \lttvClosIndCorusLo{} to \lttvClosIndCorusHi{} for the independents. CPE, read only descriptively, stayed at or above the baseline path through 2019.

\subsection{Staff counts}

For two sectors, the CRTC's staff counts allow a descriptive comparison with the last link, from revenue to jobs \citep{crtc2017sfs2016, crtc2021sfs2020}. The report gives its forecast changes in direct employment by sector against a baseline whose employment path it doesn't publish, so the comparison is with the change from 2015 and with the 2012--2015 trend carried forward, a crude stand-in for that baseline. Specialty and pay services' staff fell from \lttvStaffChanFifteen{} in 2015 to \lttvStaffChanNineteen{} in 2019, \lttvStaffChanVsTrend{} \lttvStaffChanVsTrendDir{} the trend, against a forecast shortfall in direct employment of \lttvStaffChanForecast{} FTEs by 2019. Distributors' staff stayed near its 2012--2015 trend, \lttvStaffDistVsTrendEighteen{} \lttvStaffDistVsTrendEighteenDir{} it in 2018 and \lttvStaffDistVsTrend{} \lttvStaffDistVsTrendDir{} it in 2019, against a forecast shortfall of \lttvStaffDistForecast{} FTEs by 2019 \citep[Table~22, p.~91]{nordicity2015television}. The 2019 figure is a one-year jump that reverses the next year, which may be a reporting discontinuity.

Staff counts and revenue don't move together as the report's chain implies in either sector: specialty and pay services cut staff while their revenue stayed above the baseline, and distributors' staffing stayed near trend while their revenue fell (annual series in table~\ref{tab:staff}). The mismatch can't test the report's employment prediction: staff counts aren't the report's modelled FTEs; the distributor series is labelled \enquote{Total Staff Count (FTE)} in the 2016 edition and \enquote{Total Staff Count} in the 2020 edition, and the two differ by \lttvStaffDistVintageGap{} in 2016; and a straight-line trend is a weak counterfactual. The direction of the mismatch holds with the distributors' 2018 figure in place of 2019.
